stem.en: A hunter's tool has twelve microblades set in a groove along a bone handle. One blade breaks. Why is this design better than one large stone tool at this moment?

text.en: The other blades become sharper when one of them breaks.

feedback.en: Stone does not sharpen itself. A blade stays as sharp as it was when it was struck, and then it wears down.

text.en: Only the broken blade has to be replaced, and the rest of the tool keeps working.
Microblades cannot break, so the handle must have failed.

feedback.en: The question says that a blade broke. Thin stone breaks easily, and that is why spare blades matter.

text.en: Small stone blades cut more deeply than a large tool because they weigh less.

feedback.en: Weight is not the advantage here. The advantage is that one part can be changed without making a new tool.

explanation.en: The tool is built from parts. Taking out one blade and setting a fresh one in the groove repairs the tool. The handle and the other eleven blades are kept. A large stone tool that snaps cannot be repaired in this way.

hints.en: Think about what the hunter has to throw away in each case.
